title: What the Top AI Users Are Doing Differently
dek: OpenAI's own data says the gap between the most advanced AI users and everyone else has ballooned from 2.6X in January to 8.3X by June — and the whole difference is agents. Today's episode digs into what frontier firms are actually doing differently, plus Meta's imminent consumer agent, NVIDIA as the central bank of compute, and a peek at Microsoft employees' AI bills.

oneIdea.headline: Agentic use compounds: the top AI users are pulling away from everyone else.
oneIdea.summary: In January, the most advanced AI users were using 2.6 times as much AI as average users. By the end of June, per OpenAI's own research, that gap had grown to over eight times. The reason is agents: frontier firms have moved from chat-based assistance to delegation — giving agents context, tools, plugins, and skills to do systems-level work — and because agents take on increasingly valuable work, their lead compounds. The average users just haven't made the jump, and the gap is poised to keep growing.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Usage is not outcome — an old lesson in new clothes
items.body: The whole episode rests on tokens as a proxy for work, and the counter-argument is that nobody has shown the tokens turn into anything. General practice has been here before: appointment counts, QOF points and referral rates all measured activity rather than benefit. If a practice or an ICB starts quoting AI usage figures, the sensible question is the one both sides here failed to settle — what changed for the patient, or for the clinician's day, that we can actually measure?

items.title: Where the ladder is safe to climb in a surgery
items.body: The 'use case ladder' — generation, synthesis, execution, maintenance — is a useful frame for a GP setting, and it also marks where the risk starts. Generation and synthesis are what an AI scribe already does: draft the consultation note, pull together a discharge summary. Execution and maintenance mean software acting inside the clinical record, and that is a different governance question entirely. If Zitron is right that agentic rigs need constant babysitting, the failure mode in a surgery is not lost time but a wrong entry in a live record; if the Brief is right, the gain will come from the boring end — recalls, coding, documentation — not from anything clinical.

items.title: The legal 108X figure, read from a Medical Examiner's chair
items.body: The fastest growth in agentic use is in legal work: comparing terms, flagging deviations, drafting, monitoring — with humans keeping the risk judgement and the accountability. That division of labour is precisely the one that would apply to medical examiner scrutiny or significant event work: software can read every note and flag what departs from the expected pattern, but the judgement of whether it mattered, and the signature under it, stays human. Worth watching, because the pattern arrives in medicine through the coroner's and governance side long before it arrives at the consulting room door.

the_other_side.text: Zitron attacks the same OpenAI research this edition is built on, and goes after its central instrument: the token. He argues token counts measure subsidy rather than work, since customers still "burn anywhere from $20 to $40 in tokens for every dollar of software spend", and he notes that when OpenAI and Anthropic moved larger companies onto token-based billing this year, "enterprises almost immediately started cutting token budgets" because "nobody could actually point to anything improving". He then turns OpenAI's own economists against the headline: buried on page 35 of their 69-page report is the finding that "revenue per employee is not meaningfully associated with output tokens per employee" — so a firm burning eight times the tokens is not demonstrably eight times more productive. On agents he doubts the delegation story itself, describing the typical rig as "a contrived series of harnesses, prompts, API calls and burned tokens" that "requires constant maintenance to do some stuff sometimes".

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether output tokens are a valid proxy for work done. Both accept the same facts: frontier-firm token use really has grown roughly seventeen-fold, agentic traffic really is most of enterprise output, and adoption really is lopsided between firms. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the token gap ever shows up in outputs — the specific observable is revenue, margin or headcount per employee for the heavy-agentic cohort against their sector peers over the next few years, which is precisely the correlation OpenAI's own economists could not find. The residue is pure worldview: Whittemore reads high token burn as capability being exercised, Zitron reads it as an inefficient product being subsidised. Whittemore is vindicated if the 8.3X cohort visibly outperforms on ordinary business measures once inference is no longer sold below cost; Zitron if usage stays high while performance stays flat and budgets are cut at renewal. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: neither disputes that adoption is now real, broad and very unevenly distributed. Watch for anyone publishing an outcome measure, rather than a usage measure, for the frontier cohort.

headlines.headline: Meta's consumer agent 'Hatch' is weeks away
headlines.summary: Per roadmap documents viewed by The Information, Meta is finishing a consumer agent known internally as Hatch — a streamlined, OpenClaw-style agent experience that could anchor a new AI agent subscription justifying a $200-a-month price tag for high-usage accounts. The rollout could begin as soon as this week as a preview to a small group of customers.

headlines.headline: WhatsApp becomes a multi-agent platform
headlines.summary: Meta plans a new platform on WhatsApp for third-party agent integration, letting multiple agents coordinate with each other via WhatsApp messages. It mirrors some GrokBot functionality — but this isn't cribbing, these are just interaction patterns we're likely to see much more of.

headlines.headline: Meta's 'Watermelon' model targets October
headlines.summary: Back in July, AI chief Alexandr Wang told staff that Watermelon had already caught up with GPT-55 on internal benchmarks. But the frontier has since moved with GPT-56 and will likely move again by October — so the question remains whether Meta gets closer to the frontier without actually reaching it.

headlines.headline: GrokBot sheds its $500-a-month confusion
headlines.summary: GrokBot's launch pricing was intentionally rate-limiting — users initially weren't sure whether they needed both Cursor Ultra and SuperGrok Heavy, a $500-a-month combination. As of this week it's included in the $60-a-month Cursor Pro subscription and the $100-a-month SuperGrok subscription.

headlines.headline: OpenAI's Sol price cut isn't about Anthropic — it's about the model stack
headlines.summary: GPT-56 Sol drops to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output, from $5 and $30, following cuts to Luna and Terra last month. Many read it as pressure on Anthropic ahead of its IPO, but the more likely driver: business customers won't just use the most expensive state-of-the-art model for everything anymore, and to the extent OpenAI has the compute to deliver frontier models cheaper, it makes sense to do so.

headlines.headline: Hugging Face's $13B ask comes with real revenue — and a bigger argument
headlines.summary: The company is now generating more than $150 million in annualized revenue, up 50% from two months ago, even though 97% of users access the platform entirely for free. For acquirers this isn't a revenue-multiple conversation: as the backbone of open weights challenging frontier gatekeeping, some argue it should be worth three to four times the $13 billion asking price.

headlines.headline: What is Jensen building? NVIDIA as the central bank of compute
headlines.summary: In a single week: a deal to license technology and acquire talent from Poolside, a stake in data-labeling company Mercur, and a potential investment in Perplexity at a $30 billion valuation — on top of NeoCloud stakes, land and power deals, and data center backstops. Some now conceptualize NVIDIA as the central bank of compute, standing behind the AI economy and setting the price of the key resource; comparisons range from John Malone's 1980s cable empire to Alphabet's Other Bets.

headlines.headline: Before you scream 'circular deals' — NVIDIA is tapped out at home
headlines.summary: NVIDIA doesn't operate its own fabs, so growing chip revenue is limited by supplier constraints it can't control. Turning investment outward — $42.3 billion in private companies as of March, with a higher number certain this week — supports the entire AI economy and, in turn, keeps NVIDIA's revenues strong for years to come.

headlines.headline: Taiwan charges nine in Blackwell smuggling scheme — including an NVIDIA manager
headlines.summary: Taiwanese prosecutors indicted nine people over a scheme to smuggle Blackwell 300 systems into China, including a manager in NVIDIA's distribution business and two Supermicro employees. The group allegedly ordered 130 Supermicro servers, with 74 delivered to China and 56 stopped — under 10,000 chips total, not nothing, but not enough to build a frontier training cluster.

headlines.headline: Inside Microsoft, AI spend runs from $1 to $28,000 a month
headlines.summary: A voluntary internal spreadsheet obtained by Business Insider shows extremely jagged AI usage: Azure ranged from $1 to $7,500 monthly, Cloud and AI topped out at $15,000, and one person in Customer and Partner Solutions ran up $28,000. Medians clustered around $150–$500 (Core AI the outlier at $975) — and notably, BI found no correlation between token burn and compensation or promotions.

headlines.headline: The jobs apocalypse narrative is finally losing its grip
headlines.summary: One of the best shifts in AI narratives right now is moving away from the accepted-without-question premise that AI is obviously job-destroying. Certain roles will genuinely be obviated and society should be ready to support the people affected — but the idea of a radical, rapid jobs apocalypse was never accurate.

headlines.headline: The economy just has so much inertia... we've all been too ambitious on timelines.
headlines.attribution: Sam Altman, in a recent podcast interview
headlines.summary: Altman now says he was wrong about the speed of disruption after GPT-4 — people keep buying from the same companies and using tools the same way. He calls the inertia a positive that will make the transition 'smoother and slower,' and says he's grateful for it.

headlines.headline: Who needs a pause AI movement when you've got corporations?
headlines.summary: Institutional inertia is doing the work AI doomers wished regulation would: even with incredible technology, society and the economy adapt slowly, and that slowness is the real governor on the pace of transformation.

headlines.headline: I have a better way to do it now, and I still do it the old way.
headlines.attribution: Sam Altman, on his own 'psychologically inconsistent' work habits
headlines.summary: Altman admits he's been using computers the same way for 20 years despite having 'a magic thing called Codex' — still clicking around, pasting between messaging apps, scrolling mindlessly through email. Something in his mind encodes that rote computer work is what it means to be productive, even though his stated preference is the opposite.

headlines.headline: It's not secret satisfaction — it's mind muscle memory
headlines.summary: We all get stuck in the patterns of how we've always done things. Building a new, less comfortable mind muscle feels exhausting when we know exactly how long the old way takes — which is precisely why studying the people who have broken out of that muscle memory matters so much.

headlines.headline: OpenAI buried its best enterprise research
headlines.summary: OpenAI's 'Enterprise Signals: What Frontier Firms Are Doing Differently' puts hard numbers around how leading firms use AI — and the company barely promoted it. It only surfaced widely when A16Z reposted it in their charts of the week. Great stuff; please promote it more heavily next time.

headlines.headline: Codex growth is fastest where the engineers aren't
headlines.summary: Since early February, Codex use among engineering practitioners is up 5X — but finance and accounting is up 20X, marketing and communications 26X, people/recruiting and sales each 41X, and legal a staggering 108X. As one line making the rounds put it: LLMs are for lawyers what spreadsheets were for accountants.

headlines.headline: The flippening: agentic tokens hit 64% of enterprise output
headlines.summary: In August 2025, enterprise output tokens were essentially 100% ChatGPT. By February the split was 87/13, by March 73/27, and by late April agentic crossed 53%. When OpenAI's data set ends in June, agentic work represents 64% of enterprise output tokens — meaning, using tokens as a proxy for volume of work, almost two-thirds of the work is now agentic.

headlines.headline: The frontier-firm gap exploded from 2X to 8.3X
headlines.summary: Through most of 2025, the average user at a frontier firm (top 10% of enterprises by output tokens per active user) used about twice as many tokens as one at a typical firm. The gap hit 2.6X in January and now stands at 8.3X. Overall, average firms use about twice as many tokens as 18 months ago — frontier firms use 17 times as many.

headlines.headline: Frontier firms aren't just using agents more — they're using them better
headlines.summary: At typical firms, about 9% of weekly active users use plugins and only 3% use skills; at frontier firms it's 21% and 19%. And even they haven't topped out: at OpenAI itself, 93% of employees use skills and 95% use plugins.

headlines.headline: Why coding got agents first — and why knowledge work is catching up
headlines.summary: OpenAI's diagnosis: code bases give agents clear context, tests make outputs verifiable, and progress in coding accelerates AI R&D itself. General knowledge work lagged because tasks provide limited context and lack clear verification criteria — but scaling, reinforcement learning, and evals like GDPVal are bringing real-world tasks within reach, and agentic AI has found product-market fit with general knowledge workers since the start of the year.

headlines.headline: The unlock wasn't the models — it was the patterns
headlines.summary: It's great that OpenAI is making models and harnesses work better for knowledge work, but that's not why agentic use has grown among non-engineering knowledge workers. It's grown because we've started figuring out the patterns that actually allow agents to thrive in our own contexts.

headlines.headline: The use case ladder: generation, synthesis, execution, maintenance
headlines.summary: Advanced agentic use climbs a ladder: generation (drafting emails, reports, formulas) at the base, then synthesis of disparate data sources, then execution inside existing systems, and finally maintenance — agents keeping a system running over time. Agentic use takes individual chat workflows and moves them into systems-level work that impacts more than the individual.

headlines.headline: In legal, agents own coverage — humans own risk judgment
headlines.summary: In chat, legal work is 57% writing and 20.5% knowledge retrieval. In agentic use, coding jumps to 32.9%, system operations to 17.7%, and workflow automation to 7.7% — agents comparing terms, flagging deviations, drafting red lines, and monitoring commitments, while humans keep negotiating material terms, setting risk tolerance, and owning accountability. The same pattern shows up in basically every department.

headlines.headline: The next leap is multiplayer AI, not individual AI
headlines.summary: Even frontier users climbing into execution and maintenance are mostly running agents in individual silos. The next generation of gains will come at the intersection of different teams — team AI rather than just individual AI. And with frontier firms racing ahead, the numbers should be a wake-up call for anyone not deploying agents at scale yet.
